rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: Shigella is a group of bacteria causing intestinal infection known as shigellosis or bacillary dysentery.

rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: Four Shigella species are recognised, with S. sonnei and S. flexneri the species most commonly found in the UK.

rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: Common symptoms include diarrhoea that may be bloody, stomach cramps, fever, nausea and vomiting.

rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: Symptoms usually begin one to three days after exposure but may take up to a week to appear.

rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: Most people recover within four to five days, although illness can last up to two weeks and severe cases may need hospital care.

rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: Shigella has a very low infectious dose and can spread through contaminated food, water, surfaces, poor hand hygiene or sexual contact.

rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: A person can remain infectious and capable of transmission for up to a month after illness.

rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: Cases require hygiene precautions and public-health management; work, school or nursery return is normally after at least 48 symptom-free hours.

rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: Shigellosis risk depends on species, travel, sanitation, food and water, sexual exposure, hygiene, antimicrobial resistance and host factors.

rows.source: UKHSA shigellosis prevention and public-health management
rows.verified: UKHSA Shigella evidence is organism-, exposure-, patient-, contact-, setting- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: Consumers should buy fireworks only from licensed or registered in-store and online sellers, not unknown social-media retailers.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: People under 18 cannot buy adult fireworks and category F4 fireworks are restricted to professionals.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: It is unlawful to set off or throw fireworks, including sparklers, in streets or other public places.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: The general firework curfew is 11pm to 7am, with later cut-offs for Bonfire Night, New Year, Diwali and Chinese New Year.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: Fireworks should be kept in their original packaging, dry, away from heat or ignition and locked away from children and animals.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: Users should read and understand all instructions and warnings, including the required spectator safety distance, before lighting a firework.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: Used-firework debris should be confirmed out, cooled, soaked in water, bagged and placed in the bin.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: Neighbours, farms and stables should be warned in advance, with pets kept secure and fireworks positioned away from animals and wildlife habitats.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: Firework risk depends on product category, compliance, storage, site dimensions, safety distance, user behaviour, spectators, weather and disposal.

rows.source: OPSS consumer-firework safety
rows.verified: OPSS firework evidence is product-, seller-, user-, site-, event- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
